intro: Flight attendants read passengers, handle emergencies and keep strict schedules, skills that security and public service jobs need. The closest of the 25 careers below is Transportation Security Screeners, with an 80% skill match and a BLS May 2025 median of $66,770, which is 5% more than the $63,580 flight attendants earn.
why_it_works: Every flight means safety checks, calm service in a small space and quick action if something goes wrong. O*NET rates social perceptiveness and service orientation at 3.75 out of 5 for this job and coordination at 3.62. Airport, postal and police work use the same mix of service and safety. Most matches need no new degree. The gaps are analyzing systems and maintaining equipment.
tips: Airport roles keep your travel benefits network: cargo supervisors are a 74% match.
Police work pays $76,210, which is 20% more, after academy training.
Postmasters and Mail Superintendents earn $96,660, or 52% more, and value service leadership.

faq.q: What jobs can former flight attendants do?
faq.a: The closest matches are Transportation Security Screeners (80%), aircraft cargo handling supervisors (74%) and reservation and ticket agents (73%), based on O*NET 31.0. Postal Service Clerks are 72% matched and earn $62,130, which is 2% less than the $63,580 flight attendant median.

faq.q: Which careers for flight attendants pay more?
faq.a: 10 of the 25 matches pay more. Police and detective supervisors earn $106,040 (67% more), Postmasters $96,660 (52% more) and Transit and Railroad Police $90,230 (42% more), according to BLS May 2025 data. Police roles usually need a certificate or academy first.

faq.q: Do flight attendants need more education to switch?
faq.a: For most paths, no. 18 of the 25 matches need no more education than flight attendants already have, including 8 of the top 10. In the closest match, 85% of workers have a high school diploma or the equivalent, and airport employers train new hires on the job.

faq.q: What skills should flight attendants learn?
faq.a: The skills that most often need work are systems analysis, systems evaluation, equipment maintenance and judgment and decision making. Time management already rates 3.12 out of 5 for this job in O*NET, so analysis and supervision skills are the main steps toward better-paid roles.
